questions.question: Describe one form of epigenetic modification that could alter the activation of certain genes in rabbit cells.
questions.answer: DNA methylation: methyl groups are added to cytosine bases, which switches the gene off (or histone modification such as acetylation, which switches it on).
steps: Epigenetic modification changes gene expression without changing the base sequence of DNA.

Histone modification such as acetylation loosens chromatin, so transcription factors can reach the gene and switch it on.
Either change alters which genes are transcribed in a given cell type.

questions.question: Explain how cells in the rabbit embryo become specialised after epigenetic modification.

Epigenetic modifications silence some genes (for example by methylation) and activate others.
Each cell then transcribes and translates only its active genes, producing specialised proteins.
The epigenetic pattern is copied to daughter cells during mitosis, so the specialisation is maintained.

questions.question: Explain the differences between the genetic material of a female human egg cell and a skin cell, which both contain a nucleus and the skin cell has 46 chromosomes.
questions.answer: The egg is haploid (23 chromosomes, one of each pair, from meiosis) while the skin cell is diploid (46 chromosomes, two copies of each gene, from mitosis).
steps: The egg cell is a gamete made by meiosis, so it has 23 chromosomes (haploid), one from each homologous pair.
The skin cell is a body cell made by mitosis, so it has 46 chromosomes (diploid) in homologous pairs.
The skin cell therefore has two alleles of each gene, while the egg has only one.
Crossing over and independent assortment in meiosis make each egg's allele combination different from the skin cell and from other eggs.

questions.question: Explain why the cells in the morula are genetically identical.
questions.answer: All morula cells come from repeated mitosis of one zygote; DNA is copied exactly before each division and shared equally.
steps: The morula forms by repeated mitosis of a single fertilised egg (zygote).
Before each division the DNA is replicated exactly, producing identical sister chromatids.
Mitosis separates the sister chromatids equally into two daughter nuclei, so each new cell has the same genotype.
Every cell in the morula therefore has the same genome as the original zygote.

questions.question: Describe the events that occur after a sperm cell enters an egg cell, until a zygote is formed.
questions.answer: Cortical granules block other sperm; the egg completes meiosis II; the sperm and egg nuclei fuse to form a diploid zygote.
steps: The sperm nucleus enters the egg cytoplasm after the sperm and egg membranes fuse.
Cortical granules release enzymes that change the zona pellucida, blocking other sperm (cortical reaction).
The egg completes meiosis II, forming a haploid egg nucleus.
The male and female nuclei fuse, forming a diploid zygote nucleus.

questions.question: Lipid droplets were found within 10 nm of mitochondria in mouse egg cells. Suggest why.
questions.answer: Fatty acids released from the lipid droplets are quickly transferred to nearby mitochondria, which respire them to make ATP.
steps: Lipid droplets store triglycerides as an energy reserve for the developing egg.
Lipase breaks the triglycerides down into fatty acids and glycerol near the droplet.
Fatty acids are oxidised in the mitochondria (beta-oxidation) to acetyl CoA, which enters the Krebs cycle.
Being very close shortens the diffusion distance, so fatty acids reach the mitochondria quickly and ATP supply is maintained.

questions.question: Describe the events from a pollen grain landing on the stigma to the production of a triploid endosperm nucleus and a zygote, using the ovule diagram.
questions.answer: A pollen tube grows to the ovule; one male nucleus fuses with the egg to form the zygote, and the other fuses with two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm.
steps: The pollen grain lands on the stigma, absorbs water and germinates, growing a pollen tube down the style.
The tube nucleus guides growth of the tube through the micropyle of the ovule.
The generative nucleus divides by mitosis to form two male nuclei in the pollen tube.
The tube releases the two male nuclei into the embryo sac.
One male nucleus fuses with the egg nucleus, forming a diploid zygote (2n).
The other male nucleus fuses with the two polar nuclei, forming a triploid endosperm nucleus (3n).

questions.question: Explain how a flowering plant with several ovules produces seeds that are genetically different from each other.

steps: Each ovule contains an egg cell produced by meiosis, which carries a unique combination of alleles.
Crossing over and independent assortment during meiosis create different allele combinations in each gamete.
Each pollen grain is also made by meiosis, so the male nuclei fertilising different ovules differ genetically.
Random fusion of different egg and pollen nuclei gives each seed a different combination of alleles.

questions.question: Cell A (mitosis) and cell B (meiosis) both have 12 pg of DNA at prophase. What is the DNA mass in each daughter cell at the end of mitosis and at the end of meiosis?
questions.answer: 6 pg in each daughter cell after mitosis; 3 pg in each gamete after meiosis.
steps: At prophase the DNA has already replicated, so 12 pg is the replicated amount.
Mitosis gives two daughter cells, each with half: 12 / 2 = 6 pg.
Meiosis halves DNA at meiosis I and again at meiosis II, so each gamete has 12 / 4 = 3 pg.
The mitotic daughters are diploid (6 pg) and the gametes are haploid (3 pg).

questions.question: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of the strategies used by date palms, orchids, fireweed and dandelions to promote or ensure seed production.
questions.answer: Outcrossing strategies give variation but depend on pollinators; self-fertilisation and asexual seed production ensure seeds but reduce variation and adaptability.
steps: Date palm has separate male and female plants, forcing cross-fertilisation, which increases variation and reduces harmful recessive alleles.
Disadvantage: pollen must be carried between plants, so pollination can fail and seed output is uncertain.
Orchids release chemicals that stop pollen from the same plant germinating, which prevents inbreeding but wastes some pollen.
Fireweed self-fertilises when cross-fertilisation fails, guaranteeing seeds, but offspring have less variation and may be less able to adapt.
Dandelion produces seeds from unfertilised eggs (apomixis), so seeds form without pollination, but the offspring are clones with no variation.
Overall, outcrossing gives variation and adaptability but risks failed pollination, while self-fertilisation or apomixis secures seed production at the cost of variation.

Centrioles move to opposite poles and spindle fibres begin to form between them.

questions.question: Give an example of a tissue that could be produced by mitosis in a plant.
questions.answer: Xylem tissue (phloem or epidermis are also acceptable).
steps: Mitosis in plant meristems produces new cells that can differentiate.
Those cells can differentiate into xylem vessels or phloem sieve tubes.
Xylem vessels form from specialised cells derived from meristematic divisions.
Epidermis is another tissue formed from mitotic cells.

questions.question: Give one role, other than growth or repair, for new cells produced by mitosis.
questions.answer: Asexual reproduction, producing genetically identical offspring (e.g. budding or vegetative propagation).
steps: Mitosis copies the genome exactly into each daughter cell.
In asexual reproduction, new cells form a genetically identical individual or clone.
Asexual reproduction does not involve meiosis or fertilisation.
Examples include budding in yeast and vegetative propagation in plants.

questions.question: Which statements about sperm cells are correct? 1 sperm cells are diploid; 2 the flagellum rotates using energy; 3 sperm cells have a streamlined shape to increase resistance. Options: A 1, 2 and 3; B 1 and 2 only; C 2 and 3 only; D 2 only.
questions.answer: D (2 only).
steps: Sperm cells are haploid, with one set of chromosomes, so statement 1 is wrong.
The flagellum rotates using ATP from the mitochondria in the midpiece, so statement 2 is correct.
Sperm cells are haploid because they are gametes made by meiosis.
A streamlined shape reduces resistance, not increases it, so statement 3 is wrong.

questions.question: Describe how the nucleus of a sperm cell enters an egg cell.
questions.answer: The sperm binds to the egg, acrosin digests the zona pellucida, and the sperm and egg membranes fuse so the sperm nucleus enters the egg cytoplasm.
steps: The sperm binds to the zona pellucida and egg surface membrane using specific receptor proteins.
The acrosome releases acrosin and other enzymes that digest a path through the zona pellucida.
The sperm cell surface membrane fuses with the egg cell surface membrane.
The sperm nucleus passes into the egg cytoplasm, while the tail stays outside.

questions.topic: RER and Golgi in Enzyme Production
questions.question: Describe the role of the rough endoplasmic reticulum and the Golgi apparatus in the production of the enzymes in cortical granules.
questions.answer: Ribosomes on the rough ER make the enzyme polypeptides, which are carried in vesicles to the Golgi; the Golgi modifies and packages them into cortical granules.
steps: Ribosomes on the rough ER translate mRNA into the enzyme polypeptide, which enters the ER lumen.
Transport vesicles carry the polypeptide from the rough ER to the Golgi apparatus.
The enzymes are then packaged into cortical granules that move to the cell surface.
The Golgi modifies the enzyme and packages it into cortical granules (secretory vesicles).

questions.question: Suggest how the cortical granule enzymes prevent more than one sperm nucleus entering the egg cell.
questions.answer: The enzymes are released by exocytosis and change the zona pellucida, so other sperm cannot bind or fuse with the egg.
steps: When one sperm fuses with the egg, the cortical granules move to and fuse with the egg surface membrane.
They release their enzymes by exocytosis into the space around the egg.
The enzymes modify the zona pellucida, so other sperm can no longer bind to it.
Other sperm are blocked, so only one sperm nucleus enters the egg.

questions.question: Describe what happens in anaphase of mitosis.
questions.answer: Centromeres divide and sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles by shortening spindle fibres.
steps: The centromeres divide, separating each pair of sister chromatids.
Spindle fibres attached to the centromeres shorten and pull the chromatids apart.
Anaphase is the stage where chromatids separate, and telophase follows.
The separated chromatids (now chromosomes) move towards opposite poles of the cell.

questions.question: State how the mitotic index of a tissue could be calculated.
questions.answer: Mitotic index = number of cells in mitosis / total number of cells x 100.
steps: Count the cells in mitosis under the microscope.
Count the total number of cells in the same field of view.
Counting several fields of view gives a more reliable value.
Divide the number in mitosis by the total and multiply by 100.

questions.question: Give the function of the mitochondria in the midpiece of the sperm.
questions.answer: They carry out aerobic respiration to make ATP, which powers movement of the flagellum.
steps: Mitochondria in the midpiece carry out aerobic respiration.
This releases energy to make ATP.
Without this ATP the sperm could not swim effectively.
ATP powers the motor proteins that make the flagellum rotate, so the sperm can swim to the egg.

questions.question: Give the name of a statistical test that could assess the strength of the relationship between midpiece length and swimming speed of sperm cells.
questions.answer: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (or Pearson's correlation coefficient for linear data).
steps: Both variables are continuous measurements, so a correlation test is suitable.
Pearson's correlation coefficient measures the strength of a linear relationship.
Spearman rank correlation gives a value between -1 and +1.
Spearman's rank correlation is used when the data are not normally distributed.
